analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal tax breaks for oil, gas, mining, and alternative-fuel producers.
analysis.headline: The bill to end oil, gas, and mining tax subsidies got no cosponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Representable Pete Stark's bill would have wiped out a set of long-standing tax benefits for energy and natural resource companies. It would have ended oil and gas producers' ability to immediately deduct drilling costs, ended percentage depletion for oil and gas wells, closed a loophole that lets investors deduct oil and gas losses against other income, and repealed tax credits for nonconventional and alcohol fuels plus reduced fuel tax rates. The revenue would have stayed with the Treasury instead of flowing to these industries.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers generally, because the bill would have raised revenue by ending tax deductions and credits that primarily benefit energy companies. Ordinary taxpayers who don't own oil and gas working interests would also benefit from closing a passive-loss exception available only to that industry.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the expensing of intangible drilling and development costs (Section 263(c)) and of mining exploration and development costs, deductions that let energy and mining companies write off drilling and exploration spending immediately.
It terminates the limitations on percentage depletion for oil and gas wells (Section 613 and 613A), a deduction that lets producers shield a share of gross income from tax.

It repeals the exception from the passive loss rules for working interests in oil and gas property, a carve-out that lets oil and gas investors deduct losses against income from other activities, something other passive investments do not allow.
It terminates the section 29 credit for fuels produced from a nonconventional source and repeals the alcohol fuels credit and the reduced fuel tax rates for gasohol and other alternative fuels.
Each repeal applies to taxable years beginning after enactment, so the revenue effects would begin quickly.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, mining companies, synthetic and alcohol fuel producers, and investors in oil and gas working interests would lose deductions and credits they currently claim, which would mean higher tax bills for those businesses and their investors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, mining, and fuel producers

drawbacks.text: Repealing intangible drilling cost expensing and percentage depletion would raise the after-tax cost of drilling, and domestic producers argue such provisions encourage exploration and domestic energy production; eliminating them could reduce drilling activity.

The bill repeals the alcohol fuels credit and the reduced fuel tax rates for alcohol-blended fuels, which would raise the cost of ethanol and methanol fuels relative to gasoline and could slow adoption of alternative fuels.

It terminates the nonconventional fuel credit only for facilities placed in service after enactment, but existing credit-support projects would see their competitive position change as the broader alternative-fuel tax benefits disappear.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have ended tax preferences that primarily benefit a narrow set of energy and mining industries and raised federal revenue, at the cost of higher taxes on domestic energy production and the loss of credits that supported alternative fuels like ethanol. Whether the tradeoff is worth it depends on how much weight one gives to domestic drilling incentives versus tax fairness; the bill offered no replacement incentives, simply terminating the preferences outright.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in September 1995, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Pete Stark (D-CA) introduced the Termination of Energy and Natural Resource Tax Subsidies Act of 1995 on September 12, 1995.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation, on the day of introduction.
The committee took no further action on the bill, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and mining companies, plus synthetic and alcohol fuel producers, kept every tax deduction and credit the bill would have repealed, because the bill never advanced beyond referral to committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy and mining companies kept their tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal energy and natural resource tax subsidies and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor introduced the bill in a Republican-controlled 104th Congress and drew zero cosponsors from either party, and the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed intangible drilling cost expensing, percentage depletion for oil and gas wells, and the passive-loss exception for oil and gas working interests — the core federal tax preferences for the industry. Ordinary taxpayers would have gained revenue; the industry would have paid more tax.

The bill repeals the expensing of mining exploration and development costs, ending an immediate write-off of exploration spending. The cost of mining exploration would have shifted onto company shareholders.

The bill repeals the alcohol fuels credit and reduced fuel tax rates for alcohol-blended fuels, raising the effective cost of ethanol and methanol fuels and removing a federal support the industry relied on.
The bill terminates the section 29 credit for fuels produced from nonconventional sources for facilities placed in service after enactment, eliminating a subsidy for synthetic fuel projects.

By repealing the passive loss exception for working interests, the bill closes a deduction channel available mainly to investors in oil and gas property, ending a tax advantage over other passive investments.
